title: Proposal 4: Simplify Building Permitting and Move Waterfront Permitting to Department of Buildings

context.text: This is one of five charter amendment questions placed on the November 2026 ballot by the Commission on Government Efficiency (COGE), the 2026 New York City Charter Revision Commission created by Mayor Zohran Mamdani in May 2026 and chaired by Patrick Gaspard.

question.text: Proposed Charter Amendment: Simplify Building Permitting and Move Waterfront Permitting to Department of Buildings. Create centralized construction permits hub to simplify permitting. Move waterfront permitting from Department of Small Business Services to Department of Buildings. Allow construction approval by additional Department of Buildings officials. "Yes" simplifies permitting by authorizing a centralized permitting hub, moving waterfront permitting to Department of Buildings, and allowing additional Department of Buildings officials to issue approvals. "No" leaves laws unchanged.

summary.text: The amendment would create a centralized hub through which applicants can access and manage construction-related permits and approvals across City agencies, consolidating what COGE describes as 40 separate approvals currently spread across 18 offices and agencies. It would move waterfront construction permitting from the Department of Small Business Services to the Department of Buildings, and authorize additional Department of Buildings divisions to approve certificates of occupancy.

measure.yesMeans: Amends the City Charter to authorize a centralized construction-permitting hub, move waterfront permitting to the Department of Buildings, and allow additional Department of Buildings officials to issue construction approvals.
measure.noMeans: Leaves the Charter unchanged: construction permits remain spread across separate offices and agencies, and waterfront permitting stays with the Department of Small Business Services.

argumentsFor.text: "Gotham Organization applauds the Commission's proposal to simplify and centralize the City's building permitting process. Anyone who has developed housing in New York understands how navigating approvals across numerous agencies adds unnecessary time, cost, and complexity to projects that our city urgently needs. Creating a single, coordinated permitting hub is a practical, commonsense reform that will help accelerate the delivery of affordable housing and critical infrastructure while maintaining appropriate oversight," said Brian Kelly, President of the Gotham Organization.

"Every month lost navigating approvals across multiple agencies is another month that families wait for the housing they desperately need. Creating a single, coordinated permitting process is exactly the kind of government reform that helps good projects get built faster without lowering standards," said Kirk Goodrich, President of Monadnock Development.

"For too long, outdated rules have made it harder than it needs to be to build in New York City ... Cutting nonprofit and small business procurement time by more than half, adding a formal rainy-day fund, consolidating 40 permits across 18 offices into a single hub, streamlining the use of public space, and unlocking more than $200 million in value from underutilized City property are exactly the kinds of reforms our industry has been calling for," said Carlo A. Scissura, President & CEO of the New York Building Congress.

argumentsAgainst.text: A spokesperson for City Council Speaker Julie Menin, Henry Robins, said of COGE's ballot package as a whole: "In just a few weeks, the commission developed a series of sweeping changes to city government with far-reaching implications for oversight, transparency, and public accountability."
